title: What not to put on the site for an independent hotel
metaTitle: What to leave off an independent hotel site
excerpt: Cut the drone pool film and the other souvenirs that delay a choice. Keep the room as it is and a clear way to check dates.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree, a desk with room to remove what is unnecessary.
caption: The ledge is almost bare. A hotel site can be that spare and still be complete. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to remove from a hotel site?
faqs.answer: An aerial film of the pool used as the opening. It reassures the team and does not show the bed. Replace it with a doorway photograph of the room, one sentence, and a way to check dates.

faqs.question: What else fails the same test?
faqs.answer: Logo animations, background music, email popups before the dates, stock couples, award badges you cannot explain, and a journal you will not update. Also cut a book button that opens a film, and a contact form that is easier to find than the checker.

faqs.question: How small can the finished site be?
faqs.answer: Homepage, rooms, rates, arrival, one proof about a real constraint, a short about page with names, a contact path for exceptions, and policies in the footer. Add a kitchen note only when it is true. New modules have to serve the room, the dates, or the exception.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Independent hotel website mistakes often start as things the team enjoys. The one to cut first is a drone shot of the pool used as the main argument. It reassures the people who made the site and confuses a traveler comparing three stays. Keep the room as it actually is, and keep a clear way to check dates. A shorter site that tells the truth will outperform a long site that performs taste.

Nielsen Norman Group's research explains the mechanism. Visitors often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, they read only about a quarter of the text on pages they do open, and a clear offer in the first 10 seconds is what earns any longer stay. Extra pages of mood are not a bonus. They are pages that will not be read, sitting in front of the two facts that would have been. Google's people-first guidance asks a matching question: after the visit, did the person learn enough to do the thing they came to do, or do they need to search again?

## Cut the pool film first

Remove the aerial pool sequence from the opening of the site. Not from the archive, if you love it. From the first screen, the homepage hero, and any autoplay. It does not show the bed. It does not show the light in the room. It looks like every other roof and rectangle of water the traveler has already skipped this week.

If the pool is real and bookable, keep one still, from a guest's height, on the page that mentions the pool, with the season it is open. That is information. The film was a compliment the site paid to itself. Compliments do not help a comparison.

Cutting it will feel, internally, like a loss of production value. Sit with that feeling and do it anyway. Production value is not the same as information. The traveler cannot award you a budget. They can only award you a night, and only if they understand the night.

Replace the opening with the doorway frame of the room you are willing to stand behind. One frame. A sentence. Check dates. You have just removed the most common mistake and installed the most common repair. The rest of this essay is the same test applied to everything else you are tempted to keep.

## What the team is protecting

Teams protect the pool film because it was expensive, because a relative liked it, or because it looks like the hotels in a magazine they respect. They protect a logo animation for the same reason: it was debated for weeks, so it must be important. They protect a paragraph about the founder's taste because it sounds like the meetings in which the hotel was invented.

None of these are contemptible. They are internal souvenirs. The site is not the place to store them. A souvenir reassures people who already know the property. A traveler does not know the property. Souvenirs read as delay.

Ask, of any element the team is angry to lose: does this help a stranger choose this room over two others, or check whether Friday is free? If the answer is "it expresses who we are," require a second sentence that names the guest's decision. If the second sentence cannot be written, the element is a souvenir. Thank it. Remove it from the nav and the first screen. You can keep a copy in a folder for the people who made it.

This is also how you avoid a redesign that only changes type. If the new site opens on the same film, you have reskinned the mistake. The cut list belongs in the brief, or the brief is only visual.

## What the traveler is doing

The traveler is not attending your brand. They are in a comparison. Three tabs, a date range, a budget they may not tell you, a companion with a veto. They will give you a few seconds, then a few more if the room is intelligible. Nielsen's "quarter of the text" finding means your long page is already an unread page. Write for the quarter you will get, and delete the rest, or move it behind a deliberate click.

They are also wary. They have stayed in places that photographed a pool and delivered a dark room. Your film triggers that memory even when your room is good. Honesty is not only ethical. It is how you avoid being filed with the disappointments.

The traveler's job list is short. Room, dates, price shape, arrival, a human for the exception. Anything that is not on that list needs a reason tied to a real guest question. "Because the page felt empty" is not a guest question. Empty, on a hotel site, is often the sound of a page that has finally become usable.

Do not add content to feed a search engine. Google's guidance is direct that people-first pages are the point, and that pages made to chase visits, padded to a fashionable length, or written so a reader still has to search again are the failure mode. A thin true page about the small double is better than a long page that says "luxury" twelve times and never shows the lane.

## Keep the room

What stays is the room as it is. The doorway picture. The afternoon light. The bath. The caption with the limit. The room names a guest would say. If you have three rooms, three true descriptions beat one blended dream. Blending is a common mistake: the best window from one room, the best bed from another, a bathroom you only have upstairs, presented as "our rooms."

Keep the sentence that would have prevented a bad review. The stair. The street. The shower. The size of the bed. Teams cut these sentences because they fear they will lose the booking. They lose a worse thing when they keep the booking and forfeit the guest's trust at check-in. The site's job is the right booking, not the maximum booking.

Keep photography that matches the season you are selling. A permanent June hero during a February campaign is a mistake even if the file is lovely. Swap the file. Do not rely on the guest to imagine the weather you failed to show.

If a picture exists only because the shoot day was pretty, and it hides a constraint you mention in email, the picture is a mistake. Email has become the real website. That is backwards. Put the email's honesty on the page, then the inbox can get quieter.

## Keep the way to check dates

The second thing that stays is the path to dates. A header label in plain words. A checker that does not demand an account before it shows a night. A pricing page that states what is included. A phone layout where the control is reachable and does not jump when the picture loads.

Mistakes around this path are ordinary and serious. A "Book" button that opens a film. A checker that forgets the dates when it hands off to another system. A minimum stay revealed only after the guest has entered a postal address. A contact form that is easier to find than the checker, so the desk becomes a manual booking engine and then complains about email.

Fix the path before you add features. A gift shop, a journal, a loyalty scheme, a popup. Each one competes with dates. On a small property the competition is fatal because you do not have a separate team to absorb the confusion. One path. Then exceptions.

If the checker is ugly and the rest of the site is precious, you have decorated the wrong object. Spend the care on the checker: labels, errors, the total, the room name. Beauty at the edge of a clumsy booking is a classic mistake. Guests remember the clumsy part because that is where their money moved.

## Other cuts that pass the same test

Apply the souvenir test across the site. Cut a logo animation that plays before the room. Cut background music. Cut a popup that asks for an email before dates are visible. Cut stock photographs of travelers who are not your guests. Cut award badges you cannot explain in one spoken sentence. Cut a blog you will not update, because an abandoned journal makes a living house look closed.

Cut a virtual tour that begins in the most flattering corridor and skips the stair. Cut a page for every nearby keyword you hope to rank for, if the page has nothing to say that the room page did not say. Cut "experiences" that are really a list of restaurants you do not operate. A short list of places you will genuinely help a guest reach is not a mistake. A fake concierge menu is.

Cut a second headline that restates the first in fancier words. Cut the icon row of comfort, design, and location. Cut any sentence that could be swapped onto the competitor's site without edit. Those sentences are the padding Google's guidance is skeptical of, and they are the sentences guests skip on the way to a fact. Let the fact stand alone. It will feel bare in the design file and clear on the phone.

Keep policies, but keep them as policies, linked by their names: cancellation, privacy, cookies. A mistake in the other direction is hiding the cancellation rule because it feels unfriendly. Unfriendly is a guest who could not find it. The rule can be firm and still be printed.

## A shorter site

When the cuts are done, the site should feel almost too small to the team. Homepage with room and dates. Rooms. Rates. Arrival. One proof about the real constraint. A short about page with names. A contact path for exceptions. Policies in the footer. That is a complete hotel site. You can add a note from the kitchen when you have something true to say. You do not add it to fill a template.

Read the shorter site against the quarter-of-the-text constraint. A person who reads a quarter of a short, factual page has read the decision. A person who reads a quarter of a long, tasteful page has read an adjective. Choose the first outcome.

Then stop. The ongoing mistake is to reopen the cut list every time a vendor offers a module. New modules must serve the room or the dates or the exception path. If they do not, they are the pool film in software form.

The same discipline changes when the buyer changes. A parent choosing a school is not comparing rooms for a night, and the souvenir they are protecting is different. [What a school homepage has to prove to a parent](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-an-independent-school) is the next piece, because the test stays strict and the object of the test moves from the room to the day.

If you want help holding that cut list in a redesign, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the thing the team is most proud of. The useful work often starts by asking whether a traveler can sleep in it.
